_meta.purpose: STOF XSS Vulnerability Knowledge Base -- real disclosed bug bounty patterns for stof/modules/xss_tests.py.
sources: HackerOne #1481207 (GitLab) -- Stored XSS in Notes with CSP bypass
HackerOne #2974307 (Autodesk) -- Stored XSS via forum post title, viewable by both normal and privileged users
HackerOne #485748 (X/xAI) -- Stored XSS on reports, triggers for anyone reviewing the report
A 2025 self-hosted-program disclosure -- stored XSS (unfiltered payload, weak CSP) escalated a low-priv account to full Organization Admin takeover
PortSwigger Web Security Academy -- Web message (postMessage) DOM XSS, DOM XSS source/sink fundamentals
_meta.key_finding: xss_tests.py previously only covered REFLECTED XSS (3 context variants: HTML body, attribute breakout, script/event-handler breakout) -- all same-request, response-inspection only. The single most commonly disclosed, highest-severity real pattern was STORED XSS: a payload submitted once and later rendered, unescaped, for a DIFFERENT viewer (frequently an admin/privileged user), which is how these reports repeatedly escalate to full account/org takeover. This gap is now closed as TC-128.4: `_looks_like_free_text_field`/`_second_order_plant_candidates`/`_second_order_verify_candidates` were promoted from `sqli_tests.py` to the shared `_injection_shared.py` parent both modules already import, and `xss_tests.py`'s new `_technique_stored_xss` reuses them for the exact same plant/verify shape (IDOR's chained-disclosure and SQLi's second-order technique are the other two examples of this shape in this codebase), checking for an unencoded marker reflection instead of a SQL-error fingerprint. DOM-based XSS remains an explicitly deferred, separate gap (see the `dom_based_xss` pattern below).

patterns.generalized_transformation: Submit a uniquely-tagged marker payload into a free-text field that gets STORED (comment, forum post, profile field, feedback form) rather than immediately reflected. The payload only fires later, when a DIFFERENT request -- often a different viewer/role, e.g. an admin reviewing submitted content -- renders the stored value unescaped.
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Two-act: Endpoint A stores the value (POST /comments, /profile, /feedback); Endpoint B (a listing/detail/admin-review page) later renders it back to a different viewer.
patterns.real_example: GitLab Notes (CSP-bypassing stored XSS), Autodesk forum post titles (viewable by both normal and privileged users), a 2025 disclosure where an unfiltered stored payload escalated a low-priv account to full Organization Admin takeover via an admin later viewing the submitted content.
patterns.evidence_signal: The marker planted via endpoint A reflects UNENCODED in an executable context when a SEPARATE request (ideally a different role/session) later loads endpoint B -- same unencoded-reflection check the existing TC-128.1-.3 techniques already use, just checked at a different endpoint/time than the plant.

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as xss_tests.py's _technique_stored_xss: plants a marker into a free-text-shaped POST field via a low-priv authenticated context, then checks a separate likely-privileged GET endpoint via a separate high-priv authenticated context for an unencoded reflection of that same marker, reusing reflects_unencoded() unchanged. Gated behind allow_state_changing_probes for the real plant POST, same convention as every other write-verb technique. Real-world validation against demo.testfire.net's sendFeedback (free-text fields) -> admin/admin.jsp pair produced a clean PASS (no unencoded reflection observed) -- the same pair SQLi's TC-127.6 second-order technique also got a clean negative on.

patterns.generalized_transformation: A client-side JS sink (innerHTML, document.write, eval, jQuery selector, postMessage handler) consumes attacker-controlled input (location.hash/search, a postMessage payload) with NO server round-trip at all -- entirely a browser-side execution path, so response-body inspection can never detect it (the server may never even see the payload, e.g. anything after a URL fragment `#`).
patterns.abstracted_endpoint_pattern: Any page URL, tested with a payload appended to `location.hash` and separately to `location.search` -- most commonly SPA-routing pages and any page rendering a 'welcome, {name}' or similar echo of a URL parameter client-side.
patterns.real_example: A real HackerOne-disclosed app listened for `hashchange` and dropped `location.hash` directly into a jQuery selector -- sharing a URL like `/#` triggered execution with zero server involvement. Uber and legacy Twitter both had disclosed `location.hash`-driven DOM XSS in client-side template rendering.
patterns.evidence_signal: GENUINE in-browser script execution, confirmed by actually navigating a real browser to the crafted URL and observing a triggered event -- e.g. a `confirm()`/`alert()` dialog actually firing, caught via a `page.on('dialog')` listener. This is categorically stronger evidence than every other technique in this codebase, all of which are response-inspection only (unencoded reflection, DB-error fingerprint, timing delta) -- DOM XSS is the one class where STOF's own Playwright browser can prove real execution, not just a signal consistent with it.

stof_coverage.notes: Implemented as xss_tests.py's _technique_dom_xss: navigates a real Playwright Page (an authenticated BrowserContext's own new_page(), not context.request.*) to up to 5 discovered GET endpoints, once with the marker payload appended as location.hash and once as location.search on a discovered (or plausible fallback) query parameter -- 10 navigations max. A page.on('dialog') listener is registered before each navigation and auto-dismisses immediately; a FAIL requires the dialog's message to actually contain this run's own unique marker. Real-world validation against demo.testfire.net (5 endpoints, 10 navigations) produced a clean PASS -- no DOM sink observed, consistent with this target's classic server-rendered JSP architecture (its already-confirmed TC-128.1-.3 reflected XSS findings are server round-trip, response-inspection hits, a structurally different bug class from what this technique targets).

patterns.generalized_transformation: N/A -- not a testable attack pattern for automated detection.
patterns.why_not_automatable: Self-XSS requires a human to be socially engineered into pasting attacker-supplied JavaScript into their OWN browser console (or an equivalent out-of-band action) -- there is no HTTP request/response signal, timing delta, or DOM state that distinguishes 'this input could become self-XSS' from any other input reflection, because the vulnerability isn't in what the application does with input at all -- it's in whether a human can be tricked outside the application entirely. This is precisely why every major bug bounty program (per bughunting methodology guides and program scope pages reviewed) lists self-XSS as explicitly out of scope by default, and why it only becomes a real, reportable finding when CHAINED with a second, genuinely testable vulnerability (most commonly CSRF, to force the paste/action on a victim without their knowledge -- at which point it has become CSRF-chained reflected/stored XSS, not 'self-XSS' as its own class).

stof_coverage.gap: No automated technique exists or should exist for this in isolation. If a target's CSRF findings (already covered by csrf_tests.py) ever pair with a reflected/stored XSS finding on the same state-changing action, that combination IS the real, reportable version of this pattern -- STOF already has both halves as separate confirmed findings; deliberately not building a fused 'self-XSS' technique that would just fabricate a signal that doesn't exist at the HTTP level.
